# My van almost caught fire. Here's what the electrician found, and what to check on yours

This isn't a fun post, and I almost didn't write it. But Tasha is about to put a deposit down with the same builder who did my van, and a few of you are probably thinking about builds too. So here's all of it, as plainly as I can.

**Quick note before anything else: I am not an electrician.** I'm a dog groomer. Everything below is what I was told by a licensed electrician and what I've learned since, and I've tried to get the numbers right. If something here conflicts with what a qualified person tells you about your own van, listen to them, not me. The whole point of this post is that you should get a pro to look at your setup.

## What happened

Wednesday, October 28, around 2:15 in the afternoon. I was in a client's driveway in Bedford drying Moose, a Bernese mountain dog, on high. If you've never dried a Bernese, picture a very large, very fluffy sofa that needs forty minutes of hot air.

First I smelled hot plastic. I assumed it was the dryer motor, because that's the thing that usually smells when something's off. I kept going for a few seconds, and then I saw smoke coming out of the bench seat in the back, which is where the batteries live.

I hit the battery switch, got Moose out through the side door (still damp, and honestly thrilled, he thought it was an adventure), and grabbed the extinguisher. I used a bit of it, though I'm still not sure I needed to. By the time I got back in and looked, the positive lug on the inverter cable was black, and the cable's jacket had melted back about 3 cm from it.

Everyone is fine. Moose is fine. His mom brought me a coffee and sat on her front steps with me while I shook for a good while. I'll remember that kindness for a long time.

## My setup

So you know what we're talking about:

- 3000W inverter
- Two 200Ah lithium batteries, 12V system
- Built by Coastline Van Fitouts (Darren) in spring 2025
- The dryer pulls roughly 1800 to 2000W, and sometimes the water heater is running too

The inverter is the box that turns the battery's 12V DC power into regular 120V outlet power. Anything you plug in, like a dryer, goes through it. That means all of that power has to flow from the batteries to the inverter through one pair of thick cables, and that's where my problem was.

## What the electrician found

I had Priya at Sackville Marine Electric look at the van. She went through the whole system and showed me what she was seeing as she went. Four things stood out.

### 1. The cable was too thin

The cable from the battery to the inverter was 4 AWG. Priya said that for a 3000W inverter at 12V it should have been 2/0.

If you haven't dealt with wire sizes, they're counterintuitive: a *smaller* number means a *thicker* wire. 4 AWG is a decent-sized cable, and it looks beefy if you don't know better. 2/0 (pronounced "two-aught") is much thicker again.

Here's why the size matters, in numbers. Power is volts times amps, so amps = watts ÷ volts. At 12V:

- A 3000W inverter at full tilt is about 250 amps
- My dryer at 1800 to 2000W is somewhere around 150 to 170 amps, and in real life a bit more because the inverter loses some power as heat
- Add the water heater now and then, and I was regularly somewhere in the 150 to 250 amp range

That is a *lot* of current. Low voltage means high amps for the same amount of power, which surprised me, since 12V sounds gentle. As I understand it, a 4 AWG cable is generally rated for something around 100 amps, give or take depending on the insulation and how it's installed. So I was running a cable at well over what it was meant to carry, over and over, every time I dried a big dog.

Thin wire carrying too much current heats up. That's basically how a toaster works. Nothing was wrong the first time I used it, or the fiftieth, and I think that's part of what makes this so sneaky. It just ran hot for months until something gave out.

### 2. The lug was badly crimped

The lug is the metal end piece on the cable, the part that bolts onto the inverter terminal. It's attached by crimping, meaning it's squeezed onto the wire with a big tool made for that job.

The lug on my positive cable looked like it had been crimped with pliers, or maybe even hammered. Not a proper crimping tool. And there was heat-shrink tubing over it, so I never would have seen that just by looking at my own wiring. It looked finished.

Why does that matter? A bad crimp means a poor connection between the lug and the wire, and a poor connection resists current. Resistance becomes heat, and it all happens in one small spot. That's what I think we were looking at when I found the lug black and the jacket melted back.

I can't tell you which of these problems did it, the undersized cable or the crimp. My guess is it was the combination, but that's a guess.

### 3. The fuse was in the wrong place

I did have a fuse, a 300A ANL. So I thought I was covered. But it was mounted about 90 cm (a little under three feet) from the battery. Priya said it should be within about 18 cm (roughly 7 inches).

The reason, as it was explained to me: a fuse only protects the wiring *after* it. Everything between the battery and the fuse is unprotected. If something shorts in that stretch, nothing stops the battery from pushing everything it has into it, and a lithium battery can push a *lot*. So you want the fuse as close to the battery as you can get it, to keep that unprotected stretch short. Mine had almost a meter of it.

There's a second thing here that I want to be careful about, because it's my own understanding and not something I'm quoting from Priya. A fuse is supposed to protect the *wire*. A 300A fuse is built to blow at around 300 amps. But if the cable can only safely handle about 100, then the cable can overheat at 150 or 200 amps and the fuse will sit there doing nothing, because it never sees a number big enough to care about. As far as I can tell, that's exactly what happened to me. The fuse didn't fail. It just wasn't matched to the cable it was supposed to be protecting. Ask your own electrician about this one, since it's the kind of thing that depends on the exact setup.

### 4. No smoke detector where it mattered

The only smoke detector in my van was the one in the cab, the one that came with the van. Nothing in the back, near the batteries, where this actually started. I saw the smoke because I happened to be standing right there. If I'd been in the cab, or if it had started while I was somewhere else, I'd have found out much later.

## The photo comparison

This was the part that really stuck with me. Priya pulled up my damage photos and put them next to thermal camera shots of her own van running a similar kind of load.

Hers barely gets warm. You can see the cable as a faint, mild color. Mine, well, you've seen where mine ended up. Same kind of work, same kind of power draw, completely different outcome. That difference is wild to look at. It made it very clear to me that this wasn't bad luck, and it wasn't something that "just happens" with inverters. It was about how the system was built.

## What I'm doing about it, and what it costs

The repair quote is $4,200. That covers rewiring the main runs, a new fuse block, and a class T fuse. As I understand it, class T is built to handle the huge current lithium batteries can deliver, which is why it's what you see in a lot of proper installs. The work will take 3 weeks at minimum, and the parts are on order.

My van is my whole income. So far I've cancelled 31 appointments. I've filed with my insurance, and their answer is "maybe." An adjuster is coming Thursday. Rent is due the 1st. I'm scared, honestly, and I'm trying not to spiral. To everyone I've cancelled on: I'm sorry, and thank you for being kind about it.

## About the builder

I want to be careful here, because I'm not trying to trash anyone publicly. I'll just tell you the facts and you can decide what to make of them.

Coastline Van Fitouts built my van in spring 2025. After the fire I texted Darren three times and sent one email. As of this writing I haven't heard back. I don't know why, and I'm not going to guess. That's all I'm going to say about it.

What I'll say more broadly is that I trusted the build because it *looked* tidy. Neat wiring, clean runs, everything hidden away nicely. **Tidy is not the same as right.** I couldn't tell the difference, and that's on me for not asking harder questions. That's the lesson I want you to take from this, especially if you're not an electrical person either.

## For Tasha, and anyone getting a build done

Tasha, this one's especially for you. You're about to put a deposit down, so before you do:

**Ask the builder for cable sizes and fuse specs in writing.** Not a promise, not "yeah, it's all proper." An actual written list. Here's what I'd ask for:

- What size cable is used for each main run (battery to inverter, battery to fuse block, and so on), and why that size for your inverter and your loads?
- What fuses are going in, what are their ratings, and where exactly will they be mounted? How far from the battery?
- What tool is used to crimp the lugs?
- Is there a wiring diagram you can keep?
- Does a licensed electrician do the work or sign off on it?
- What does the warranty cover, in writing, and what happens if something goes wrong?

Then think about how they react. A good builder who knows their stuff shouldn't mind these questions at all. If they get defensive or vague about basic numbers, that tells you something. And if you get the answers and you still can't tell whether they're right, pay an electrician for an hour to read them over. That's cheap compared to what I'm looking at.

## Get a cheap infrared thermometer

Everybody with a van like this should own one. I picked mine up at Canadian Tire for about $40. It's a point-and-shoot gadget that reads the surface temperature of whatever you aim it at, from a distance, no touching.

The idea is simple. Run your normal heavy load, like the dryer, for a while, then aim it at the cable, the lugs, the fuse, and the inverter connections. Compare them to each other and to the room. You're looking for *anything that's noticeably hotter than everything around it*. Priya's cable barely got warm. If yours is way hotter than that, or one connection is hot while the rest are fine, stop and get someone to look at it.

I'm not giving you a magic number, because I'm not qualified to, and the right answer depends on your setup. Ask your electrician what normal looks like for your van. And if you smell hot plastic, don't take a reading, just shut everything down.

## A checklist you can do yourself, with the power off

None of this replaces a professional, but you can do it in an afternoon with a flashlight, a tape measure, and your phone for photos.

**Before you start:** turn off your battery switch and unplug everything. One thing I want to be clear about, because it matters: the switch only cuts power to what's *after* it. The batteries themselves are still live, and so is anything wired directly to them before the switch or fuse. So **just look and measure. Don't loosen, tighten, or poke around with tools near the battery terminals**, and take rings and bracelets off. If something needs to be touched or adjusted, that's a job for your electrician.

**Cables**
- [ ] Find the big cable running from the batteries to the inverter. Most cable has its size printed on the jacket (look for "AWG" or something like "2/0"). Write it down, and take a photo.
- [ ] Check your inverter's manual for the recommended cable size. Does your cable match?
- [ ] Look along the whole length for discolored, soft, or deformed jacket, anything that looks melted or shiny.

**Lugs and connections**
- [ ] Look at the lugs at both ends of each big cable. Does the crimp look like it was done with a proper tool (clean, even, consistent), or does it look pinched, flattened, or beat up?
- [ ] Is there heat-shrink over the crimp? If so, you can't see the work underneath. Ask whoever built it, or an electrician, whether it's been done properly.
- [ ] Look for any black marks, melted plastic, or green or white crust around the terminals.

**Fuses**
- [ ] Find the main fuse. Write down the type and rating printed on it.
- [ ] Measure from the battery's positive terminal to the fuse. Is it close, in the neighborhood of that 18 cm / 7 inch mark, or is it far away like mine was?
- [ ] Ask your electrician whether the fuse rating actually matches the cable it protects.

**Safety gear**
- [ ] Is there a smoke detector in the back, near the batteries and not just in the cab? If not, put one there.
- [ ] Is your extinguisher easy to grab, and do you know where it is without looking?
- [ ] Do you know exactly where the battery switch is, and can you reach it fast, even in a panic?

**Paperwork**
- [ ] Do you have the cable sizes, fuse specs, and a wiring diagram in writing from your builder? If not, ask for them.

**Then, with the power back on**
- [ ] Run a normal heavy load for a good while, then use your infrared thermometer on the cables, lugs, fuse, and inverter connections.
- [ ] Anything noticeably hotter than the rest? Anything that smells off, flickers, or makes the inverter fan scream? Stop and call someone.

And one more time: **if any of this looks wrong, or if you just can't tell, get a qualified electrician to look at it.** You can't fully judge this stuff by eye. I know that better than most people now.

## Where I'm at

The van is off the road. The repair is booked, the parts are on order, and it'll be three weeks at the very least. I'm waiting on the adjuster Thursday, and I don't know yet what insurance will cover. Rent's due the 1st, I've got 31 cancelled appointments behind me, and I'm doing my best to stay calm about it. Some days that works better than others.

I'm also really glad I'm writing this to you from my couch and not from a hospital. It could have gone so much worse, and I know that.

I'll post again once the van's back on the road, and I'll let you know how the repair went, what the insurance said, and what the new setup looks like. Until then, go check your cables. Please.

Take care of each other, and your vans.

---

A few things to check before you post:

- **Timing:** you wrote "last week," but Oct 28 is two weeks before today (Nov 11), so I wrote "two weeks ago" in the title. Change it if I've got your timeline wrong.
- **Not from your notes:** the point that a 300A fuse won't protect a cable only good for about 100A, and the "roughly 100 amps" ballpark for 4 AWG, are general electrical knowledge I added. I flagged them in the post as your own understanding, but it's worth confirming both with Priya.
- **Names:** I named Darren and Coastline since your notes did and Tasha's readers will want to know. If you'd rather not, or want to run it past your insurer first, they're easy to cut. The Darren section sticks to what happened (three texts, one email, no reply) with no guesses about why.
